title: HE LOOKED AT HER BREASTS AND COMPARED THEM TO TWO YOUNG GAZELLES. WHY IS THIS IN THE HOLY BIBLE?
paragraphs: HE LOOKED AT HER BREASTS AND COMPARED THEM TO TWO YOUNG GAZELLES. WHY IS THIS IN THE HOLY BIBLE?
Song of Songs 4:5 — The Scripture That Makes Some Christians Uncomfortable, the Beauty God Never Called Dirty, and the Gospel That Restores What Shame Has Stolen.
There is a verse in your Bible that some Christians would be embarrassed to read aloud in church.
Not because it contains profanity.
Not because it celebrates sin.
But because a man looks at the woman he loves, admires her breasts, and describes them with astonishing tenderness.
And the Holy Spirit allowed those words to remain in Scripture.
For thousands of years.
Think about that.
The same Bible that commands us to flee sexual immorality contains a love poem in which a man openly delights in the physical beauty of his beloved.
The same God who calls His people to holiness preserved a passage that many religious people would rather skip.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question isn't why God allowed such language into His Word.
Perhaps it's why so many of us have learned to feel ashamed of something God originally created good.
Because somewhere between Eden and our broken world, something happened to the human heart.
Love became confused with lust.
Beauty became confused with temptation.
Intimacy became confused with exploitation.
And shame began speaking so loudly that even God's beautiful design could sound scandalous.
But what if this verse is not an embarrassment to explain away?
What if it is an invitation to recover something we have almost forgotten?
Something about love.
Something about the body.
Something about holiness.
And ultimately, something about the grace of Jesus Christ.
Stay with me, because the deeper we enter this passage, the more clearly we will see why the Bible refuses to surrender the beauty of love to the ugliness of sin.
Song of Songs 4:5 says:
“Thy two breasts are like two young roes that are twins, which feed among the lilies.” — Song of Solomon 4:5, KJV
Yes.
That is actually in the Bible.
And no, we do not need to apologize for it.
But we do need to understand it.
Because Scripture deserves more than a nervous laugh, a provocative headline, or a shallow interpretation.
It deserves reverence.
And the people whose hearts have been wounded by distorted ideas of love deserve to hear what God actually says.
In the original Hebrew, the verse reads:
שְׁנֵי שָׁדַיִךְ כִּשְׁנֵי עֳפָרִים תְּאוֹמֵי צְבִיָּה הָרוֹעִים בַּשּׁוֹשַׁנִּים
Shenei shadayikh kishnei ofarim, te'omei tseviyyah, haro'im bashoshanim.
A close English rendering is:
“Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, grazing among the lilies.”
The Hebrew word שָׁדַיִךְ (shadayikh) means “your breasts.”
The word עֳפָרִים (ofarim) refers to young deer or fawns.
תְּאוֹמֵי (te'omei) means “twins of,” emphasizing the paired imagery.
And צְבִיָּה (tseviyyah) refers to a female gazelle.
The final image, הָרוֹעִים בַּשּׁוֹשַׁנִּים (haro'im bashoshanim), describes them grazing among lilies, though the precise botanical identity of the Hebrew shoshanim is debated.
The picture is pastoral, gentle, graceful, and alive.
In the ancient poetic world of the Song, gazelles evoke beauty, elegance, tenderness, and graceful movement.
The lover is not giving an anatomical lecture.
He is writing poetry.
He sees beauty in the woman he loves, and he reaches into the natural world for language worthy of his admiration.
And here is something important.
He is not speaking about a nameless body.
He is addressing his beloved.
The surrounding verses describe her eyes, hair, teeth, lips, temples, and neck through a series of imaginative comparisons.
Her beauty is celebrated through the language of an intimate relationship.
This is not a stranger being reduced to a collection of body parts.
It is the voice of a lover expressing delight.
And the distinction matters.
Because the Bible does not teach that sexual desire is inherently sinful. It teaches that desire must be governed by love, faithfulness, and holiness.
That truth may challenge the person who has spent years believing that any acknowledgment of physical beauty is automatically impure.
But it also challenges the person who uses physical attraction as an excuse to objectify, manipulate, or consume another human being.
Scripture refuses both distortions.
And that is where this ancient poem begins to speak with startling relevance to our modern lives.
We live in a world where bodies are displayed everywhere, yet people are increasingly afraid they are not beautiful enough.
A world where intimacy is advertised constantly, yet genuine tenderness can feel painfully rare.
A world where someone can receive a thousand compliments about their appearance and still go to bed wondering whether anyone truly loves them.
Perhaps you know that feeling.
Perhaps someone once told you that you were beautiful, but their actions eventually revealed that they only wanted access to your body.
Perhaps you trusted someone who promised love but left you carrying shame.
Perhaps you gave your affection to someone who treated your vulnerability like an opportunity.
Or perhaps you have been on the other side.
You have looked at people without honoring their humanity.
You have confused attraction with entitlement.
You have allowed pornography, fantasy, comparison, or selfish desire to shape the way you see another person.
And now, when you encounter a verse like Song of Songs 4:5, you are forced to confront a question that goes deeper than the verse itself.
Have I learned to see another human being as someone to cherish, or merely someone to desire?
Because those are not the same thing.
And the difference can change a life.
Long before the Song of Songs was written, the opening chapters of Genesis described a world where the human body was not an object of shame.
Genesis 1:27 declares that God created humanity in His image, male and female.
Genesis 1:31 tells us that God saw everything He had made, and it was very good.
Then Genesis 2:25 gives us an extraordinary picture:
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.”
Read that slowly.
Naked.
And not ashamed.
There was no need to pretend.
No fear of being used.
No suspicion that vulnerability would become a weapon.
No comparison with another person's body.
No anxiety that love would disappear when physical beauty changed.
The man and woman stood before each other without the fear that now haunts so many relationships.
But then sin entered the story.
And one of the first things Adam and Eve experienced was shame.
Genesis 3:7 says their eyes were opened, they knew they were naked, and they made coverings for themselves.
Their bodies had not suddenly become evil.
What had changed was their condition before God and one another.
Innocence had been shattered.
Trust had been wounded.
Sin had introduced fear, alienation, and hiding.
And humanity has been struggling with those consequences ever since.
We cover more than our bodies.
We cover our disappointments.
Our insecurities.
Our secret addictions.
Our memories.
Our regrets.
Our desperate longing to be loved without being rejected.
Some people hide behind religious performance.
Some hide behind sexual attention.
Some hide behind emotional distance.
Some hide behind the appearance of a perfect marriage.
And some have become so accustomed to being treated carelessly that genuine affection feels suspicious.
This is why the Song of Songs matters.
It reminds us that sin did not erase God's original goodness from creation.
The beauty of faithful love is still worth celebrating.
The body is still part of God's good creation.
Tenderness is still possible.
Delight is not automatically defilement.
And holiness does not require us to despise what God has made.
Yet we must also understand what the Song is, and what it is not.
Song of Songs is Hebrew love poetry.
It contains intimate dialogue, longing, admiration, separation, reunion, and rich imagery drawn from nature.
Jewish and Christian interpreters have long discussed its meaning.
Some have emphasized its celebration of human love and marriage.
Others have also understood it allegorically or spiritually, seeing in the lovers' relationship a reflection of God's covenant love for His people or Christ's love for the Church.
These interpretations have a long history, but they should not be confused with the direct literary meaning of every image.
Song of Songs 4:5 is, in its immediate context, a lover's poetic description of his beloved's physical beauty.
It does not directly say that the two breasts symbolize the Old and New Testaments, the two covenants, or any other specific spiritual pair.
Such interpretations may appear in historical allegorical readings, but the Hebrew text itself does not establish them.
We honor Scripture by refusing to make it say what it does not say.
And we honor Christ by recognizing how the whole biblical story ultimately reveals the goodness of creation, the devastation of sin, and the hope of redemption.
The beauty of the Song does not need to be erased in order for us to discover its place in the larger story of God's love.
Consider another remarkable statement from this same biblical book.
Song of Songs 8:7 declares:
“Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.”
That is not a description of disposable affection.
It is a poetic celebration of love's extraordinary strength.
And Song of Songs 8:6 speaks of love as strong as death, with a flame-like intensity that cannot be treated casually.
This is a very different vision from the one our culture frequently sells.
Our world often says, “I want you because of what you can give me.”
Faithful love says, “Your well-being matters to me.”
Lust without love asks, “How can I satisfy myself?”
Love shaped by holiness asks, “How can I honor you before God?”
And that distinction becomes even clearer when we turn to Jesus.
Think about the way Christ treated people whom society had reduced to their failures.
In John 4, Jesus met a Samaritan woman at a well.
He knew the complicated history of her relationships.
He did not pretend her story was irrelevant.
But neither did He treat her as someone unworthy of conversation, truth, or grace.
He spoke to her about living water.
He revealed that He was the Messiah.
And the woman who came to the well carrying a complicated personal history went back to her community speaking about the One who knew her.
She said:
“Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?” — John 4:29, KJV
There is something deeply moving about that moment.
Jesus knew.
And He still spoke to her.
He knew her history.
And He still offered living water.
He did not need to exploit her vulnerability to demonstrate His authority.
He met her with truth.
And with grace.
Maybe that is the part of the Gospel you need to hear today.
Because some people have been told they are no longer worthy of love because of what happened to them.
Some carry guilt over sexual sins they committed willingly.
Others carry shame for violations committed against them, even though the wrongdoing was never theirs.
Those are not the same experiences.
And Scripture must never be used to place the guilt of an abuser upon the person who was harmed.
If someone violated your dignity, their sin does not make you spiritually dirty.
And if you have sinned, your failure does not place you beyond the reach of Christ's forgiveness.
The Gospel speaks truthfully to both woundedness and guilt without confusing them.
Jesus does not call evil good.
But He also does not declare that every broken person must remain broken forever.
This is why the cross matters.
Not because Jesus came merely to improve our self-esteem.
Not because He came to reassure us that our choices have no consequences.
But because our sin is real, our need for reconciliation with God is real, and His mercy is greater than we could ever deserve.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we fixed every habit.
Not after we learned how to appear holy in public.
Christ died for sinners.
And His resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
That is the difference between a temporary emotional experience and the transforming power of the Gospel.
Jesus does not simply tell us that we are loved.
He calls us to repent, believe, follow Him, and receive new life through His grace.
And that new life changes how we see other people.
It changes how we treat their bodies.
It changes how we understand intimacy.
It changes what we do when temptation comes.
It changes the way we love someone who has trusted us with their heart.
Consider the words of 1 Corinthians 6:19–20:

“What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.”
The Apostle Paul is addressing believers and calling them to honor God with their bodies.
He does not describe the body as worthless.
He teaches that it matters profoundly.
So much so that our physical conduct belongs within our worship.
And suddenly the supposed contradiction begins to disappear.
Song of Songs celebrates the beauty of embodied love.
First Corinthians calls believers to embodied holiness.
These truths are not enemies.
They belong together.
God's design for sexual intimacy is not that people should feel nothing.
It is that desire should not become a master that destroys love, faithfulness, and obedience.
The Bible's vision is neither prudish contempt for the body nor unrestricted indulgence of every impulse.
It is something richer.
A love that can delight without degrading.
A desire that can honor boundaries.
An intimacy that is not separated from covenant faithfulness.
A tenderness that refuses to turn another person's vulnerability into a transaction.
And this matters whether you are married, single, widowed, divorced, or carrying the pain of a relationship that did not survive.
Your worth before God is not determined by whether someone finds you sexually attractive.
You do not become less human because you are unmarried.
You do not become less deserving of dignity because your body has aged.
You do not lose the image of God because of scars, disability, illness, infertility, or changes in appearance.
And you do not need another person's desire to prove that your life has meaning.
Physical beauty has a place in the Song of Songs.
But it is not the foundation of human worth.
That foundation is deeper.
You were made in the image of God.
And the call of Christ is not to worship beauty, but to worship the Creator.
For married couples, this passage offers a particular challenge.
When was the last time you looked at your spouse with genuine appreciation rather than silent criticism?
When was the last time your words made them feel cherished rather than evaluated?
When was the last time affection was given freely, without manipulation or pressure?
Perhaps the person beside you has changed since the day you first met.
There are new wrinkles.
New scars.
New responsibilities.
Perhaps childbirth, sickness, exhaustion, financial hardship, or years of sacrifice have altered the body you once knew.
And perhaps the world keeps whispering that beauty belongs only to the young, the flawless, and the endlessly desirable.
But faithful love learns to recognize beauty that cannot be captured by a photograph.
It sees the hands that worked when the family had little.
The face that stayed awake beside a hospital bed.
The body that carried burdens nobody else noticed.
The person who remained when life became difficult.
Song of Songs 4:5 celebrates physical beauty, and we should not pretend otherwise.
But the broader biblical call to covenant love challenges us to cherish the whole person through every season of life.
Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
Notice the standard.
Not domination.
Not entitlement.
Not self-centered pleasure.
Sacrificial love.
Christ gave Himself.
And although human marriage can never perfectly reproduce the love of Christ, Christian husbands are called to reflect His self-giving care.
That means tenderness without coercion.
Affection without humiliation.
Faithfulness without double lives.
Repentance when wrong has been done.
And a willingness to serve rather than merely demand.
For anyone who has used Scripture to excuse control, abuse, or sexual entitlement, this is a necessary correction.
The Bible's celebration of marital intimacy never gives permission to disregard another person's dignity, safety, or consent.
Love does not become holy simply because someone attaches God's name to it.
Its character must agree with God's commands.
And perhaps, as you read this, you realize the deepest problem is not what someone else has done.
Perhaps you recognize your own sin.
Maybe you have been feeding desires that are destroying your ability to love faithfully.
Maybe pornography has trained your eyes to see people as images rather than neighbors.
Maybe you have been flirting with betrayal while telling yourself that nothing serious has happened.
Maybe you have been comparing your spouse to strangers.
Maybe you have convinced yourself that because temptation is common, surrender is inevitable.
But temptation does not have to become obedience to sin.
And shame does not have to become your permanent identity.
The Gospel does not invite you to hide more skillfully.
It invites you to come into the light.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That promise is not permission to continue carelessly.
It is an invitation to genuine confession and repentance.
And sometimes repentance will require difficult, practical steps.
Ending a secret relationship.
Seeking accountability.
Removing access to material that feeds destructive habits.
Confessing wrongdoing to someone you have harmed.
Seeking wise pastoral guidance or professional help when necessary.
Accepting consequences instead of demanding immediate trust.
Grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace makes a new beginning possible.
And perhaps the most powerful transformation is not simply that you stop looking at something sinful.
Perhaps it is that, through the work of God's Spirit, you begin learning how to see people rightly.
Not as possessions.
Not as trophies.
Not as objects created to satisfy you.
But as human beings bearing the image of their Creator.
That is a beautiful kind of freedom.
And it brings us back to the verse that started everything.
“Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, grazing among the lilies.”
What an unexpected place to begin a conversation about holiness.
Yet that is part of the beauty of Scripture.
God's Word does not require us to pretend that physical attraction does not exist.
It teaches us to understand it within the larger purposes of creation, covenant, and obedience.
The lover's admiration is not a command for every reader to speak in the same metaphors.
Nor is it permission to direct intimate language toward anyone we happen to find attractive.
It is a poetic moment within a biblical love song.
And when we respect its context, we can appreciate its beauty without turning it into either scandal or spectacle.
There is another line in this same chapter that deserves our attention.
Song of Songs 4:7 says:
“Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee.”
Within the poem, these are words of affectionate admiration spoken by the lover.
They should not be turned into a claim that his beloved was literally sinless.
Nor should we pretend that the verse directly describes Christ declaring sinners righteous.
But within the whole Christian story, those words can awaken a longing for something that human romance alone cannot give us.
To be fully known.
To be received without deception.
To be freed from the guilt we cannot remove by ourselves.
To stand before God, not because we have manufactured our own perfection, but because Jesus Christ has become our Savior.
And that hope is not found in a romantic partner.
It is found in Christ.
Second Corinthians 5:21 declares:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
Here is the greater wonder.
The sinless Savior took upon Himself the judgment our sins deserved.
He died.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith is offered forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
Not because sin was harmless.
But because His sacrifice was sufficient.
That is the grace that can reach into the most complicated human story.
The woman who has been told she is undesirable.
The husband who knows he has neglected his wife.
The single believer struggling with loneliness.
The person fighting a secret addiction.
The survivor learning that another person's cruelty does not define their worth.
The Christian who has become more skilled at hiding sin than confessing it.
The person who wonders whether God could possibly receive them after everything they have done.
The Gospel does not promise that every relationship will be restored.
It does not promise that every wound will disappear overnight.
And it does not promise that repentance will erase every earthly consequence.
But it does proclaim that forgiveness is available through Jesus Christ, and that His Spirit is able to transform those who belong to Him.
That is not a small promise.
That is resurrection hope.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not for the sake of religious performance.
Not because a comment section can measure the condition of your soul.
But because sometimes putting a struggle into words helps us stop pretending it does not exist.
What has been harder for you: believing that your body is part of God's good creation, learning to honor other people with purity, or accepting that Christ can forgive your past?
You do not have to share private details or disclose wounds you are not ready to discuss.
And if this passage has changed the way you understand biblical love, tell us what stood out to you.
Your reflection may help another person realize they are not alone in seeking truth, healing, and obedience.
Because this is not merely about one surprising verse.
It is about the way we read the Bible.
The way we see people.
The way we approach marriage.
The way we respond to temptation.
The way we carry shame.
And the way we understand the redeeming work of Jesus Christ.
There are people who have abandoned Scripture because they thought Christianity could offer only condemnation for their brokenness.
There are others who have embraced a distorted version of Christianity that excuses whatever their desires demand.
Both need the truth.
God's grace is not contempt for human weakness.
And God's holiness is not permission to redefine sin.
In Jesus Christ, grace and truth meet.
John 1:14 describes the incarnate Word as “full of grace and truth.”
We need both.
Truth without grace can be used to crush the wounded.
A counterfeit grace without truth can leave people trapped in the very sins destroying them.
But Christ calls us into the light where sin can be confessed, forgiveness received, and lives transformed.
That is the message Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim.
Not to sensationalize Scripture.
Not to build a following around controversy.
But to help people encounter the living Christ through the faithful teaching of His Word.
And if this article has helped you understand a passage you once found confusing, uncomfortable, or embarrassing, consider what might happen if it reached someone else.
Someone who believes their body is disgusting.
Someone who thinks holiness means despising physical affection.
Someone who has confused lust with love.
Someone who is afraid their past has disqualified them from grace.
Someone who has never heard that Jesus receives repentant sinners.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
But because a simple act of sharing can place biblical truth before someone who might never intentionally search for it.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who feel spiritually exhausted, seekers who have difficult questions, and even people who do not yet believe in Jesus to follow along.
They do not need to pretend they have everything figured out before they can begin reading God's Word.
We glorify God through faith in Christ, worship, obedience, generosity, service, and love—not through a mandatory payment to any ministry.
But freely chosen financial support can be a genuine expression of Christian generosity.
Just as believers have supported the work of Gospel ministry throughout history, you can choose to help sustain the creation and distribution of Scripture-centered teaching today.
If you already give to your local church, this invitation is not meant to replace your responsibilities there.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit of this invitation.
Not pressure.
Not fear.
But willing partnership in a mission you believe is worth supporting.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment and spiritual encouragement accessible.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
A deeper commitment to Scripture.
A growing hunger for Christ.
A community of believers seeking to become more faithful, more discerning, more prayerful, and more willing to live what they profess.
The Gospel is not merchandise.
The invitation to repent and believe is freely proclaimed to everyone.
And that is precisely why we want this message to reach farther.
Because someone is still hiding.
Someone is still ashamed.
Someone is still mistaking attention for love.
Someone is still trying to become worthy of a grace that can never be earned.
Someone is still reading the Bible through the lens of wounds that have never healed.
And perhaps that someone is you.
A man looks at his beloved.
He sees her beauty.
And he describes it with the language of young gazelles among the lilies.
What once sounded scandalous becomes something different when we understand its place in Scripture.
It becomes a reminder that God created the human body good.
That sin corrupts what God made beautiful.
That holiness protects rather than despises God's design.
That love is more than appetite.
That faithfulness is more than a feeling.
And that the deepest restoration we need is found not in being desired by another human being, but in being reconciled to the God who made us.
The Song of Songs does not tell the whole story of redemption.
But it belongs to the Bible that does.
And that Bible leads us to Jesus Christ.
The One who entered our broken world.
The One who never sinned.
The One who loved with perfect holiness.
The One who gave His life for sinners.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who still calls us to turn from sin and follow Him.
So if you have been using desire to fill a spiritual emptiness, come to Christ.
If you have been hiding behind shame, bring your burdens to Him.
If you have harmed someone, repent and take responsibility.
If you have been wounded, remember that what happened to you does not erase your God-given dignity.
If your marriage has grown cold, ask God to teach you how to love with renewed tenderness and faithfulness.
And if you have never surrendered your life to Jesus, do not mistake admiration for Christian teaching with saving faith.
Come to the Savior Himself.
Trust His finished work.
Turn from sin.
Receive His mercy.
And follow Him.
Because the greatest love story in Scripture is not merely about a man admiring the beauty of a woman.
It is about the holy God who did not abandon His saving purpose when humanity fell into sin.
It is about the Son of God who came to redeem sinners at the cost of His own blood.
And it is about the hope that those who belong to Christ will one day dwell with Him in a creation where sin, death, and shame are no more.
If this truth has reached your heart, do not let it remain only a passing emotion.
Respond to God in prayer.
Open His Word again.
And remember the difference between being admired and being redeemed.
A human lover may see beauty in you for a season, but only Jesus Christ can save your soul for eternity.
